idiom_name: struct Service<R: Repo> with new(repo: R, clock: Clock)
implementation_notes: Rust injects by handing a value to a constructor: struct Service<R: Repo> { repo: R } with impl Service<R> { fn new(repo: R, clock: Clock) -> Self }, traits declaring the seam and main (or a setup function) owning the concrete graph. Generic parameters give static dispatch with zero runtime cost and let the compiler reject an unsatisfied contract; the cost is that the bound propagates through every type that forwards the dependency. There is no reflection, so container crates such as shaku are compile-time macro libraries and remain optional.
pitfalls: Trait bounds grow through every struct that forwards the dependency; box it or keep generics shallow when parameter lists explode.
A shared dependency must satisfy Send + Sync + 'static (Arc<dyn Trait>), otherwise it cannot cross thread boundaries.
Interior mutability: dependencies shared behind Arc<Mutex<_>> reintroduce lock contention - prefer immutable state and &self methods.

variants.name: Type-erased Arc<dyn Trait> injection
variants.idiom_name: Arc<dyn Repo + Send + Sync> constructor injection and sharing
variants.implementation_notes: Storing Arc<dyn Repo> instead of a generic parameter erases the concrete type: one Service type serves every implementation, clones share one instance, and the implementation can be chosen at start-up (configuration or feature flag). The cost is a vtable indirection per call, heap allocation and object-safe traits; prefer it for shared services (caches, clients) and plugin-style selection, and keep generics for hot monomorphic paths. shaku's derive macros build the same structure with a module registry when the wiring itself should be generated.
pitfalls: Every implementor must be object-safe (no generic methods, no Self return) - trait design changes when a type is erased.
Erasing the type also removes monomorphisation: keep generics on hot paths where the vtable cost matters.
